**Patient Vignette: Marcus**

Marcus is a 49-year-old married man, a partner in a respected architectural firm, who presents for therapy at his wife’s urging. He is tall, with a graying beard and the measured, deliberate speech of someone used to being in control. He sits forward in his chair, hands clasped, as if preparing to defend a design concept. He describes his life as “fine,” but the word carries no conviction.

The trauma happened eighteen months ago, on a clear Tuesday morning. Marcus was on site, overseeing the final inspection of a new mixed-use development—a project he had designed from the ground up. He was standing on the second-floor balcony with the general contractor, a man named Dave, whom he had worked with for over a decade. They were discussing the railing’s sightlines. Dave was leaning back, gesturing at the skyline, when the temporary scaffolding beneath him gave way. Marcus remembers the sound first—a sharp, metallic groan, then a wet, percussive crack. He watched Dave fall two stories, landing on a pile of rebar and concrete forms. He saw the unnatural angle of Dave’s leg, the blood spreading like a slow stain on the gray dust. He heard Dave’s scream, then the silence.

Marcus froze. He did not scream. He did not run. He stood on that balcony, perfectly still, his hands gripping the railing so hard his knuckles went white. He remembers thinking, *This is not a building. This is a body.* He called 911. He waited. He told the paramedics where to find Dave. He gave a statement to the site safety officer. He did not cry. He did not shake. He went home that night, showered, and told his wife, “There was an accident. Dave fell. He’s in the ICU.”

For the first three months, Marcus threw himself into work. He redesigned the scaffolding protocol for the entire firm. He wrote a 40-page safety manual. He stayed late, often until midnight, poring over blueprints, checking load calculations. His wife, Sarah, would find him at his desk at 3 a.m., staring at a blank screen. He told her he was fine. He told himself he was fine.

But he was not fine. He stopped going to the gym. He stopped eating lunch with colleagues. He began to avoid the office’s floor-to-ceiling windows, preferring the interior conference rooms. He stopped driving his usual route to work because it passed the construction site. He took back roads, adding 20 minutes to his commute. He started checking the locks on his front door three times before bed. He became obsessed with the structural integrity of his own home—checking the foundation, the roof trusses, the load-bearing walls.

The nightmares started around month four. They are not about Dave. They are about falling. He dreams he is standing on a high ledge, or on a balcony, or on the roof of his own house, and the ground is dissolving beneath him. He wakes up gasping, sheets soaked in sweat, heart pounding. He cannot fall back asleep. He lies there, cataloging the sounds of the house—the creak of the floorboards, the hum of the furnace—certain that something is about to give way.

He has become hypervigilant in ways that confuse him. At a restaurant, he cannot sit with his back to the door. In a parking garage, he walks close to the wall, away from the edge. He has stopped attending his daughter’s soccer games because the bleachers feel unstable. He knows this is irrational. He is an architect. He understands load distribution. He knows the bleachers are safe. But his body does not care. His body remembers the sound of metal groaning.

His marriage is strained. Sarah tries to talk to him, but he deflects. He feels irritable, short-tempered. He snapped at her last week when she asked him to pick up milk. He apologized, but the apology felt hollow. He feels disconnected from his children, from his work, from himself. He used to love the feeling of a building taking shape. Now, when he looks at a structure, he only sees the potential for collapse.

He is here because Sarah said, “I can’t watch you disappear anymore.” He doesn’t know if therapy will help. He doesn’t know if anything will. He just knows that for the first time in his life, the ground beneath him does not feel solid. And he is terrified of what might happen if he stops holding it up.
